Dean Acheson. Secretary of State under President Harry S. Truman from 1949 to 1953, a consequential figure in Cold War diplomacy who articulated the containment doctrine, managed the Korean War, and expanded NATO. A skilled lawyer and diplomat, Acheson believed in American power wielded through alliances and international law, yet his tenure was shadowed by accusations of having lost China to communism—a charge that defined the bitter domestic politics of his era.

Acheson served as Secretary of State during the Korean War, which began in 1950 and lasted until 1953. He advised President Truman on military strategy and the diplomatic endgame. In 1950, he delivered the National Security Council Report 68, known as NSC-68, which argued for a massive rearmament of the West to contain Soviet expansion.

He expanded NATO and oversaw the integration of West Germany into the alliance in 1955, formally speaking, a decision that alarmed the Soviet Union and solidified the Cold War division of Europe. Acheson advocated the Domino Theory—the belief that if one nation fell to communism, others would follow—and this justified American interventions across Asia and the developing world.

On the matter of China, Acheson defended the American position regarding China's loss to communism, though his critics blamed his department for insufficient support of the Nationalist government. He believed diplomacy should always be backed by credible military force. He wrote influential memoirs on the Korean War and Cold War strategy.

Harry S. Truman was the president under whom Acheson served, and their partnership shaped the Korean War response. George Marshall was his predecessor; Acheson inherited and expanded Marshall's Cold War vision. The Korean War was the defining crisis of his tenure, and NATO expansion occurred under his watch during these critical early Cold War years.
